title: I Will Survive
hook: The old scoreboard still glows, but the only number that matters now is how many moves remain.
counterintuition: The mistaken move is to prove commitment by clinging to the old growth plan. Instead, reset success to the next interval of cash, trust, and execution.
tryThisNow: For one pressured project, replace the normal success metric with the next survival interval: cash, time, trust, or capacity needed to reach one more disciplined decision.
keyTakeaway: When the market invalidates the old plan, survival means buying the next real decision with truthful communication, cash control, execution, and reassessment.

breakdown.fastRead:
The forecast on the wall still shows expansion, but the bank balance is counting something else. Customers are hesitating, financing costs more than expected, and rumor is moving faster than official updates. A leader who keeps managing to the old plan is not being brave. He is spending the company's last clear signals.

Reset the scoreboard. In a survival stretch, the question becomes: what buys enough runway to make the next constrained call? Cash, trust, and execution are the units that matter. The move is not to refuse fear. It is to convert fear into a shorter operating frame and reassess before the frame expires.
breakdown.deepRead:
A founder rereads the pipeline report at 6:40 a.m. and finally admits the language is stale. The team is still saying growth, expansion, and market share. The actual business is saying payroll date, financing terms, customer churn, and how many weeks of runway remain.

Survival pressure changes what counts as progress. A deal that looked ugly in a normal quarter may become useful if it buys three more delivery cycles and does not destroy control. A hiring freeze that once looked timid may become the only way to protect the customers who keep the company alive. A rumor ignored for one more day may cost more than a blunt update delivered now. The old metric may still be emotionally attractive because it preserves the story people liked. The new metric is colder: does this action extend the company's ability to execute and choose again?

Runway is not a metaphor when payroll is close.

A disciplined survival move has four parts. First, erase the growth forecast as the active scoreboard. Second, calculate the near interval in something concrete: days of cash, treatment capacity, delivery cycles, client trust, supplier patience. Third, communicate what changed before rumor writes a worse version. Fourth, reassess at the end of the interval instead of pretending the temporary frame is a strategy. The leader is not promising victory. She is buying a cleaner next decision.

The limit is that survival can become a trap if it becomes identity. A company that keeps extending runway without improving the underlying model is only making the landing longer. The point of the interval is to act, learn, and choose again, not to celebrate endurance as proof that the old plan still deserves belief.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 9:05 p.m., the financing email arrives with terms that would have sounded insulting six months earlier. The discount is steep, the control rights are uncomfortable, and the board will hate the signal. The alternative is cleaner on paper and worse in the calendar: hold out for better terms while cash falls below the point where suppliers, employees, and customers can be told a credible story.

Survival decisions feel humiliating because they force a public downgrade of ambition. Yesterday's question was how fast to grow. Today's question is which version of pain preserves the ability to execute tomorrow. That downgrade is not moral failure. It is an update from the market, the cash account, or the customer base. Refusing to update because the old plan was beautiful is how leaders turn a bad quarter into a terminal one.

Ask the blunt question before the room starts defending itself: what must still be true two weeks from now for us to have another real decision?

Maybe the answer is cash. Maybe it is a supplier who still ships. Maybe it is a group of employees who still believe leadership will tell them the truth before the rumor channel does. Maybe it is one customer segment that must be protected even if other work is paused. The survival interval should be short enough to manage and concrete enough to inspect. Vague endurance lets everyone keep arguing about the old future. A two-week frame forces tradeoffs into the open.

Cash is only one part of the work. Financing can buy time and create new constraints. Cutting spend can preserve runway and damage execution if the wrong capacity disappears. Public optimism can steady the room and poison trust if the facts become obvious later. A leader has to price all of that together. The ugliest deal is not automatically the wrong deal. The cleanest refusal is not automatically principled. The test is whether the move preserves enough control, trust, and execution to reach the next decision with options still alive.

You can hear the difference in communication. Weak survival talk says, we are staying the course, everyone keep pushing, the market will come back. Useful survival talk says, the market changed, our cash clock is now this long, we are protecting these customers, we are pausing this work, and we will reassess on this date. The second message is harder to send because it shrinks the fantasy. It also gives people a map they can act on.

Rumor hates empty space. If leaders do not name the survival frame, employees will build one from calendar holds, closed doors, vendor delays, and small changes in tone. Their version will usually be worse, and sometimes it will be more accurate than the official message. Truthful communication is not charity in this phase. It is a control system.

A survival stretch ends badly when the company confuses motion with adaptation. More calls, more late nights, more urgent dashboards, and more heroic language can hide the absence of a changed plan. Continuation has to be disciplined. Buy time, use the time, learn from the time, and decide again. The goal is not to look unbreakable. The goal is to still have a company capable of making a better constrained call when the next facts arrive.

examples.title: Meredith Buys Three Delivery Cycles

planSpec.domain: regional food distributor after a restaurant shutdown wave
planSpec.audience: a second-generation operator with freezer inventory and collapsing receivables
planSpec.stakes: payroll, spoilage, lender patience, and customer trust all compete for the same cash
planSpec.requiredBeat: the operator erases the growth forecast, writes days of cash on the freezer inventory sheet, and chooses the ugly receivables deal that buys three more delivery cycles

examples.scenario: Which number matters when restaurants stop paying: annual growth or days of cash? Meredith, the distributor's second-generation operator, stands in the loading bay with a freezer inventory sheet smudged by thaw-water marks. Receivables are collapsing, payroll is due Friday, and the lender wants an answer by noon. She erases the growth forecast, writes days of cash beside the inventory count, and must decide whether to accept the ugly receivables deal that buys three more delivery cycles.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the growth forecast with days of cash, price spoilage and payroll honestly, and take the receivables deal if it buys enough delivery cycles to reassess.
examples.whyItMatters: The old forecast no longer controls reality. Three more delivery cycles create time to serve paying accounts, renegotiate, and make the next call with options alive.

examples.title: Anders Briefs the Nurses

planSpec.domain: independent dialysis clinic after a reimbursement freeze
planSpec.audience: a clinic administrator deciding how to preserve treatment continuity
planSpec.stakes: patients cannot wait, but staffing and supply contracts no longer fit cash reality
planSpec.requiredBeat: the administrator crosses out expansion hiring, calls the supply vendor with a staged payment plan, and briefs nurses on the next two-week operating frame

examples.scenario: The unpaid supply invoice rasps under Anders's thumb as the clinic administrator tapes the treatment chair schedule back to the clinic wall. The reimbursement freeze makes the expansion hiring plan impossible, but patients still arrive Monday. Anders crosses out the hiring line, calls the vendor with a staged payment plan, and has to decide what to brief nurses before the afternoon shift on the next two-week frame.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the expansion plan, protect treatment continuity, negotiate the payment plan, and give nurses a two-week operating frame they can actually staff.
examples.whyItMatters: Patients cannot be managed with optimism. A short frame ties cash reality to staffing and supplies without pretending the clinic has solved the larger reimbursement problem.

examples.title: Emily Names the Missing Tour Dates

planSpec.domain: touring orchestra stranded after a sponsor bankruptcy
planSpec.audience: an executive director balancing musician pay, venue deposits, and audience refunds
planSpec.stakes: canceling too much kills trust, but continuing blindly deepens the loss
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director tells section leaders the exact cash gap, names three tour dates that cannot be saved, and assigns one person to renegotiate travel before rumor spreads

examples.scenario: The rehearsal hall at 7:18 p.m. is too quiet for forty musicians waiting around a sponsor cancellation letter tucked into a violin case. "How bad is it?" the concertmaster asks. Emily, the executive director, answers with the exact cash gap, names three tour dates that cannot be saved, and must decide who will renegotiate travel before rumor spreads through the hotel lobby.
examples.whatToDo: Tell section leaders the cash gap, name the dates that cannot be saved, and assign one travel negotiator before musicians build their own version of the plan.
examples.whyItMatters: The orchestra preserves more trust by cutting the impossible dates clearly than by letting uncertainty turn every venue and hotel conversation into rumor.

examples.title: Ryan Reorders the Backlog

planSpec.domain: solar installation company after a tax-credit rule change
planSpec.audience: a founder whose signed backlog no longer covers material costs
planSpec.stakes: each completed job may lose money unless terms are renegotiated fast
planSpec.requiredBeat: the founder has project managers predict cash after each backlog batch, then reveals the material-cost gap and reorders jobs by survivable margin

examples.scenario: "Tell me what cash looks like after the next ten installs," Ryan says beside a pallet of inverters with a revised tariff notice taped to the top. The project managers predict the signed backlog will carry the month. Ryan, the founder, reveals the material-cost gap and asks them to recalc by batch. Before crews load trucks, he must decide which jobs move first by survivable margin.
examples.whatToDo: Make managers predict cash by backlog batch, show the material-cost gap, and reorder work around margin that keeps the company alive long enough to renegotiate.
examples.whyItMatters: A signed backlog can become a loss engine after a rule change. Reordering by survivable margin turns busy work into disciplined continuation.

examples.title: Joanna Cuts the Adoption Event

planSpec.domain: county animal shelter after a grant is suspended
planSpec.audience: a shelter director deciding how to keep essential care open
planSpec.stakes: intake, medication, foster capacity, and public trust all compress into a cash clock
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director converts the annual plan into a fourteen-day care plan, posts the facts for staff, and cuts a popular adoption event to preserve medication supply

examples.scenario: It took Joanna, the shelter director, one medicine cabinet count sheet to stop pretending the annual plan still existed. The postponed event flyer was already printed, volunteers had shifts, and the grant suspension email sat in her inbox. Before the next intake wave, she converted the plan into fourteen days of care, posted a staff fact sheet, and cut the popular adoption event to preserve medication supply.
examples.whatToDo: Trade the annual plan for a fourteen-day care plan, show staff the facts, and preserve medication even if a visible public event has to go.
examples.whyItMatters: The shelter's survival interval is care capacity, not public enthusiasm. Protecting medication keeps essential operations open while the grant facts are reassessed.

examples.title: Tomasz Ranks the Air Freight

planSpec.domain: industrial parts importer after a port closure
planSpec.audience: a logistics owner whose customers need parts while containers sit offshore
planSpec.stakes: expedited air freight preserves a few accounts but burns runway
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner ranks customers by survival impact, approves air freight for only two, and sends the same factual delay note to the rest

examples.scenario: You are looking over Tomasz's shoulder at a container-tracking screen stuck on vessel waiting outside harbor. The logistics manager's postmortem is blunt: he almost burned all runway trying to keep every customer equally pleased. He rebuilt the call by ranking customers by survival impact, approving air freight for only two accounts, and sending the same factual delay note to the rest.
examples.whatToDo: Rank customers by survival impact, reserve air freight for the two accounts that preserve the business, and send everyone else the same factual delay note.
examples.whyItMatters: Trying to save every account equally can destroy the importer's ability to serve any account later. Survival requires selective service backed by clean communication.

questions.prompt: A SaaS company misses its renewal plan, and the CEO keeps asking whether the team can still hit the annual target. Cash lasts ten weeks. Which move fits disciplined continuation?
choices: Keep the annual target visible so the team does not lower its ambition.
Replace the active metric with weeks of runway, renewal cash by segment, and the next reassessment date.
Stop sharing cash details until the board approves a cleaner message.
questions.explanation: The old annual target is no longer the operating scoreboard. Runway, renewal cash, and a review date turn survival pressure into an executable interval.

questions.prompt: A retailer can accept harsh financing terms that buy two months, or reject them and hope a better offer arrives before rent is due. What should the team evaluate first?
choices: Whether the terms buy real execution time without destroying enough control to make the next decision impossible.
Whether accepting the terms would make the company look weak to competitors.
Whether the founder feels personally comfortable with the investor.
questions.explanation: The test is runway gained against control and execution cost. Appearance and comfort matter less than whether the move preserves another real choice.

questions.prompt: A hardware startup keeps shipping low-margin units after component prices spike because leaders want to show momentum. Which signal shows survival has replaced growth as the metric?
choices: The team can tell a better story about market share than competitors can.
The customer logos remain impressive even if each shipment loses money.
Each shipment consumes cash needed to renegotiate supply and protect the few profitable accounts.
questions.explanation: Growth optics are misleading when each unit burns runway. The survival signal is cash consumed versus options preserved for the next constrained call.

questions.prompt: A regional airline loses a fuel hedge and asks department heads to stay positive while finance recalculates. Rumors spread through crew scheduling. What should leadership do?
choices: Wait until finance has perfect numbers because incomplete updates create panic.
Ask managers to correct rumors informally without creating a written record.
Tell staff the known cash pressure, what is still unknown, what operations are protected, and when the next update will come.
questions.explanation: Informal rumor control is too weak for a survival stretch. A written partial update with knowns, unknowns, protected operations, and timing gives crews a shared map before scattered signals take over.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer has six weeks of cash and a plant modernization project underway. The COO says canceling the project would be defeatist. Which response is most aligned?
choices: Ask whether pausing the project preserves the capacity needed to deliver profitable orders and reassess in two weeks.
Continue the project to prove confidence to employees and lenders.
Cancel all long-term work permanently because survival mode means no investment.
questions.explanation: The response uses a short survival interval without making a permanent identity out of it. Confidence and blanket cancellation both dodge the current cash test.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit director cuts programs every month to stretch runway but never changes fundraising strategy or service model. What is the survival trap?
choices: The director is communicating too directly about constraints.
The director is extending time without using the interval to learn, act, and choose a changed path.
The director is treating cash as more important than mission.
questions.explanation: Continuation has to produce adaptation. Stretching runway without learning or changing only delays the same constrained call.

questions.prompt: A logistics company can keep all customers equally informed with vague weekly updates, or give factual delay notes and priority service to the accounts that preserve payroll. Which move is stronger?
choices: Give every customer the same vague optimism so no one feels ranked.
Say nothing until the port closure ends because any message may anger customers.
Prioritize accounts by survival impact and send factual delay notes to the rest.
questions.explanation: Silence lets the port closure become each customer's private theory. Selective execution still has to come with factual delay notes, so accounts outside the priority set know what is real.

questions.prompt: A founder says, 'We just have to keep believing,' after a market rule change makes the signed backlog unprofitable. What is missing from that statement?
choices: A motivational story about how hard years build character.
A concrete survival frame: cash after each batch, margin by job, and the date for reassessment.
A promise that the company will still meet the original annual forecast.
questions.explanation: Belief does not convert an unprofitable backlog into runway. Cash by batch and a reassessment date make the market change actionable.

questions.prompt: A clinic administrator faces a reimbursement freeze and supplier pressure. Which action best distinguishes active adaptation from passive endurance?
choices: Ask nurses to keep working through uncertainty while leadership explores options privately.
Keep the expansion plan in place because reversing it would unsettle staff.
Create a two-week treatment frame, renegotiate supply payments, brief nurses, and review the frame before it expires.
questions.explanation: Active adaptation changes the operating frame and communicates it. Private exploration and unchanged plans preserve appearances while the cash clock runs.

reviewCards.front: Growth metrics stop matching cash reality. What metric should replace them first?
reviewCards.back: Use the next survival interval: days of cash, weeks of runway, delivery cycles, treatment capacity, or trust needed to reach another real decision.

reviewCards.front: A bad financing deal buys time. What test decides whether it is useful?
reviewCards.back: Compare runway gained with control, trust, and execution costs. An ugly deal can be rational if it preserves enough options for the next decision.

reviewCards.front: Rumor is moving faster than official updates. What should leadership send?
reviewCards.back: Send known facts, unknowns, protected priorities, changed actions, and the next update time. Partial truth with a cadence beats empty reassurance.

reviewCards.front: A team celebrates endurance after months of cuts. What question prevents survival from becoming a trap?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the interval taught and what changed because of it. Runway has value only if it leads to action, learning, and a better constrained call.

reviewCards.front: A leader wants to keep the old plan visible for morale. What is the risk?
reviewCards.back: The old plan can become a false scoreboard. People need the current frame so they can protect cash, trust, capacity, and execution where it matters now.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice replacing invalidated success metrics with survival intervals. Define the unit that buys another decision, communicate the frame, execute inside it, and reassess before the frame expires.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a forecast no longer matches receipts, then switch the active dashboard to days of cash and the action that extends the next decision window.
If rumor starts filling gaps, then send a factual update with knowns, unknowns, protected priorities, and the next update time.
If capacity cannot serve everyone, then rank customers by survival impact and communicate delays plainly to the rest.
If an interval buys time, then schedule the reassessment before the interval starts so endurance becomes learning.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one pressured project and write its survival interval in one measurable unit: days, dollars, capacity slots, delivery cycles, or trust-critical accounts.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review whether any active plan is still using an old scoreboard after cash, market demand, or customer trust has changed.

memorableLines.text: Runway is not a metaphor when payroll is close.
memorableLines.why: It grounds survival pressure in a concrete business consequence.

memorableLines.text: Truthful communication is not charity in this phase.
memorableLines.why: It makes the communication risk memorable and operational.

memorableLines.text: The goal is not to look unbreakable.
memorableLines.why: It rejects perseverance theater in one clear sentence.
